task: A 67-year-old woman comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. She had a pulmonary embolism and required treatment in the hospital for 3 weeks. She had a retroperitoneal hemorrhage; anticoagulant therapy was temporarily discontinued, and she underwent placement of an inferior vena cava (IVC) filter. She had a hematoma that was resolving on discharge from the hospital 2 weeks ago. Today, she says she has had a persistent sensation of tingling and numbness of her left thigh that she did not report in the hospital because she thought it would go away; the sensation has improved somewhat during the past week. Her only medication is warfarin. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination of the skin shows no abnormalities. Muscle strength is normal. Sensation to light touch is decreased over a 5 x 5-cm area on the lateral aspect of the left anterior thigh. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's decreased sensation? A: Cerebral infarction during the hospitalization, B: Complication of the IVC filter placement, C: Compression of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, D: Hematoma of the left thigh

The patient's symptoms of tingling and numbness localized to the lateral aspect of the left anterior thigh are highly suggestive of a sensory deficit involving the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (LFCN). This nerve is a branch of the lumbar plexus and supplies sensation to the lateral thigh. The LFCN is particularly vulnerable to compression, especially in the region of the inguinal ligament.

The patient had a retroperitoneal hemorrhage, which led to temporary discontinuation of anticoagulation and placement of an IVC filter. During this time, she developed a hematoma that was resolving at discharge. It is possible that the hematoma or the procedure related to the IVC filter placement caused direct compression of the LFCN, leading to its entrapment and subsequent sensory loss.

While other options such as cerebral infarction or hematoma of the left thigh are possible, they do not account for the specific localization of the sensory deficit. A hematoma of the thigh would more likely present with pain, swelling, and possibly motor weakness, rather than isolated sensory loss. Cerebral infarction would typically present with more widespread neurological deficits.
